subject: social
chapter: History IV · The Age of Industrialisation
source: NCERT India and the Contemporary World II (Class X History), Chapter IV

topics.name: Before the Industrial Revolution and the coming of the factory
The pace of change, hand labour and workers’ lives
Factories come up; peculiarities of industrial growth

questions.q: Industrial production for an international market before factories is called –
questions.a: proto-industrialisation
questions.e: ‘Proto’ means the first or early form of something.

questions.q: Why could merchants not expand production within European towns?
questions.a: Urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful
w: Factories had taken over the towns
questions.e: Guilds controlled production, competition and prices and restricted entry.

questions.q: Who created the cotton mill?
questions.a: Richard Arkwright
questions.e: Costly new machines could be set up and maintained in the mill.

questions.q: The earliest factories in England came up by the –
questions.e: Their number multiplied only in the late 18th century.

questions.q: Which city came to be known as a ‘finishing centre’ for cloth?
questions.a: London
questions.e: Finishing was done in London before the export merchant sold the cloth.

questions.q: Why did poor peasants eagerly agree to produce for merchants?
questions.a: Common lands were enclosed and tiny plots could not support the household; merchant advances gave extra income
w: They wanted to move to cities
questions.e: They could stay in the countryside and use family labour fully.

questions.q: Britain’s raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to –
questions.a: 22 million pounds in 1787
questions.e: Linked to inventions that improved carding, twisting, spinning and rolling.

questions.q: Which was an advantage of bringing all processes under one roof in a mill?
questions.a: Careful supervision of production, a watch over quality and regulation of labour
w: Workers could choose their own hours
Machines became cheaper than hand tools
questions.e: This had been difficult when production was in the countryside.

questions.q: In the proto-industrial system each merchant employed 20–25 workers at each stage. This meant –
questions.a: each clothier controlled hundreds of workers
w: each worker controlled hundreds of merchants
questions.e: The system was controlled by merchants, with goods made in family farms.

questions.q: Arrange the stages in the work of an English merchant clothier: (i) dyers (ii) wool from a stapler (iii) spinners (iv) weavers and fullers
questions.a: (ii) → (iii) → (iv) → (i)
questions.e: Stapler → spinners → weavers → fullers → dyers; finishing in London.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Histories of industrialisation that begin with factories miss an important phase. Reason (R): Large-scale production for an international market existed before factories. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
w: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.e: That phase is proto-industrialisation.

questions.q: Up to the 1840s, the leading sector in Britain’s first phase of industrialisation was –
questions.a: cotton
questions.e: After that iron and steel led the way.

questions.q: Who improved Newcomen’s steam engine and patented it in 1781?
questions.a: James Watt
questions.e: His friend Mathew Boulton manufactured it but found few buyers.

questions.q: The Spinning Jenny was devised in 1764 by –
questions.a: James Hargreaves
questions.e: One wheel set many spindles in motion.

questions.q: At the beginning of the 19th century there were no more than how many steam engines in all of England?
questions.e: 80 in cotton, 9 in wool, the rest in mining, canal works and iron works.

questions.q: In mid-19th-century Britain, how many varieties of hammers were produced?
questions.e: And 45 kinds of axes – these needed human skill.

questions.q: By 1873 Britain’s export of iron and steel was worth about –
questions.a: £77 million, double the value of its cotton export
w: the same as its cotton export
questions.e: Railway expansion raised demand for iron and steel.

questions.q: At the end of the 19th century, what share of Britain’s workforce was in technologically advanced industrial sectors?
questions.a: Less than 20 per cent
questions.e: New industries could not easily displace traditional ones.

questions.q: Why did industrialists in Victorian Britain prefer hand labour?
questions.a: Labour was plentiful and cheap, demand was seasonal, and many products needed skill
questions.e: In America, with labour shortage, mechanisation was preferred.

questions.q: Why did the upper classes in Victorian Britain prefer hand-made goods?
questions.a: They symbolised refinement and class – better finished, individually produced and carefully designed
questions.e: Machine-made goods were for export to the colonies.

questions.q: Which industries needed extra workers in the cold months or before Christmas?
questions.a: Gas works, breweries, book-binders and printers
questions.e: Industrialists employed workers for the season.

questions.q: In periods of economic slump like the 1830s, the proportion of unemployed went up to –
questions.a: between 35 and 75 per cent in different regions
questions.e: At the best of times about 10 per cent of the urban population were extremely poor.

questions.q: Why did the colliers’ wives want to destroy the new machine?
questions.a: They had lost their work to spinning engines and feared less demand for manual labour
questions.e: Women who survived on hand spinning attacked the Spinning Jenny.
questions.passage: A magistrate reported in 1790: ‘From the depredations of a lawless Banditti of colliers and their wives, for the wives had lost their work to spinning engines … they advanced at first with much insolence, avowing their intention of cutting to pieces the machine lately introduced in the woollen manufacture; which they suppose, if generally adopted, will lessen the demand for manual labour.’

questions.q: Why do wage rates tell us little about workers’ welfare in early 19th-century Britain?
questions.a: Averages hide variations; prices rose in the Napoleonic War; and income depended on the number of days of work
w: Workers were paid only in food
questions.e: Real value of wages fell when prices rose sharply.

questions.q: After the 1840s, why did employment opportunities grow in British cities?
questions.a: Building activity intensified – roads, railway stations, tunnels, drainage and sewers
questions.e: Transport workers doubled in the 1840s and doubled again in 30 years.

questions.q: Before the age of machine industries, which country dominated the international market in silk and cotton textiles?
questions.a: India
questions.e: The finer varieties often came from India.

questions.q: A paid servant appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers was called a –
questions.a: gomastha
questions.e: He collected supplies and examined the quality of cloth.

questions.q: The gross value of trade through Surat fell from Rs 16 million (late 17th century) to –
questions.a: Rs 3 million by the 1740s
questions.e: Old ports declined as European companies gained power.

questions.q: As Surat and Hoogly decayed, which ports grew?
questions.a: Bombay and Calcutta
questions.e: An indicator of the growth of colonial power.

questions.q: In 1811–12 piece-goods were 33 per cent of India’s exports. By 1850–51 they were –
questions.a: no more than 3 per cent
questions.e: The beginning of a long decline.

questions.q: Which was NOT a step taken by the East India Company to control weavers?
questions.a: Allowing weavers to sell to the highest bidder
w: Giving advances that tied weavers to the Company
questions.e: The Company prevented weavers from dealing with other buyers.

questions.q: Why did weavers clash with gomasthas?
questions.a: Gomasthas were outsiders who acted arrogantly, came with sepoys and peons and punished weavers for delays
w: Gomasthas lived in the weaving villages
questions.e: Earlier supply merchants had close ties with the villages.

questions.q: By 1850 cotton piece-goods were over 31 per cent of the value of Indian imports; by the 1870s they were –
questions.a: over 50 per cent
questions.e: At the end of the 18th century there had been virtually no such imports.

questions.q: Cotton weavers in India faced two problems at the same time in the early 19th century. They were –
questions.a: the export market collapsed and the local market was glutted with Manchester imports
w: too many orders and too few looms
questions.e: Machine-made imports were so cheap that weavers could not compete.

questions.q: How did the American Civil War affect Indian weavers in the 1860s?
questions.a: Raw cotton exports to Britain rose, prices shot up and weavers were starved of supplies
w: It created a huge market for Indian cloth in America
It lowered the price of raw cotton
It stopped Manchester imports into India
questions.e: Weaving could not pay.

questions.q: Why had the cloth trade at Jahanabad ceased, according to the Commissioner of Patna?
questions.a: Cheap and durable Manchester goods could not be competed with
questions.e: Deindustrialisation in Gangetic Bihar.
questions.passage: The Commissioner of Patna wrote: ‘It appears that twenty years ago, a brisk trade was carried on in the manufacture of cloth at Jahanabad, and Behar, which has in the former place entirely ceased, while in the latter the amount of manufacture is very limited, in consequence of the cheap and durable goods from Manchester with which the Native manufactures are unable to compete.’

questions.q: How did weavers in Carnatic and Bengal respond to Company control?
questions.a: Some deserted villages, some revolted with village traders, and many refused loans and became agricultural labourers
w: They all joined the Company army
They set up cotton mills in Bombay
questions.e: They lost the space to bargain for prices.

questions.q: In 1772 Henry Patullo said demand for Indian textiles could never reduce. Why was he proved wrong?
questions.a: British industrialists won import duties at home and pushed Manchester goods into Indian markets
w: The French bought all Indian cloth
questions.e: Exports declined from the beginning of the 19th century.

questions.q: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in –
questions.e: It went into production two years later.

questions.q: The first iron and steel works in India was set up at Jamshedpur in 1912 by –
questions.a: J.N. Tata
questions.e: Iron and steel started much later than textiles.

questions.q: An old and trusted worker employed by industrialists to recruit new workers was called a –
questions.a: jobber
questions.e: He gradually began demanding money and gifts.

questions.q: Over 50 per cent of workers in Bombay cotton industries in 1911 came from –
questions.a: Ratnagiri
questions.e: In most regions workers came from nearby districts.

questions.q: Seth Hukumchand set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in –
questions.e: He was a Marwari businessman who also traded with China.

questions.q: Which of these was NOT a European Managing Agency?
questions.a: Tata and Sons
questions.e: These Agencies dominated Indian industry till the First World War.

questions.q: How did many early Indian industrialists accumulate capital?
questions.a: Through trade with China – opium and tea – and raw cotton shipments
questions.e: Dwarkanath Tagore, Dinshaw Petit and J.N. Tata.

questions.q: Why did early Indian cotton mills produce coarse yarn rather than fabric?
questions.a: To avoid competing with Manchester goods, since yarn was not an important British import
w: Yarn was the only thing Indians wore
questions.e: The yarn was used by handloom weavers or exported to China.

questions.q: Why did Indian industrialists shift from yarn to cloth after 1906?
questions.a: Chinese and Japanese mills flooded the Chinese market, cutting Indian yarn exports – and swadeshi boosted cloth demand
questions.e: Cotton piece-goods production in India doubled between 1900 and 1912.

questions.q: Why did industrial production in India increase during the First World War?
questions.a: Manchester imports declined and Indian mills supplied the home market and war needs
w: Britain sent new machines to India
questions.e: Jute bags, uniform cloth, tents, boots, saddles.

questions.q: What share of the total industrial labour force worked in registered factories in 1911 and 1931?
questions.a: 5 per cent and 10 per cent
questions.e: The rest worked in small workshops and household units.

questions.q: By 1941 over what share of handlooms in India had fly shuttles?
questions.a: Over 35 per cent
questions.e: In Travancore, Madras, Mysore, Cochin and Bengal it was 70 to 80 per cent.

questions.q: According to Vasant Parkar, how were millworkers linked to their villages?
questions.a: They went home for harvest and sowing, and mills granted leave for it
w: They never returned to their villages
They sent their land to the jobber
They lived permanently in mill housing
questions.e: Workers moved between village and city.
questions.passage: Vasant Parkar, once a millworker in Bombay, said: ‘The workers would pay the jobbers money to get their sons work in the mill … The mill worker was closely associated with his village, physically and emotionally. He would go home to cut the harvest and for sowing. The Konkani would go home to cut the paddy and the Ghati, the sugarcane. It was an accepted practice for which the mills granted leave.’

questions.q: Why did weavers of finer cloth survive better than those producing coarse cloth?
questions.a: Demand for fine cloth from the well-to-do was stable, and mills could not imitate specialised weaves
w: Fine cloth was made in factories
The poor bought more fine cloth in famines
questions.e: Banarasi and Baluchari saris, Madras lungis and handkerchiefs.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Handloom cloth production almost trebled between 1900 and 1940. Reason (R): Weavers adopted new technology like the fly shuttle that raised productivity without excessively raising costs. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A
w: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.e: Handicrafts expanded even in the age of factories.

questions.q: When buyers saw which words on cloth labels, they were expected to feel confident about quality?
questions.a: ‘MADE IN MANCHESTER’
questions.e: Labels made the place of manufacture and company familiar.

questions.q: Why were calendars a good way to advertise in India?
questions.a: They were used even by people who could not read and were seen every day
w: They were printed in Manchester only
questions.e: Hung in tea shops, poor homes, offices and apartments.

questions.q: Why did Manchester labels carry images of Indian gods and goddesses?
questions.a: To give divine approval and make foreign goods appear familiar
w: To show the goods were made in temples
questions.e: Kartika, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Krishna.

questions.q: What message did advertisements of Indian manufacturers carry?
questions.a: If you care for the nation, buy products that Indians produce – swadeshi
questions.e: Advertisements became a vehicle of the nationalist message.

questions.q: Why were figures of emperors and nawabs used in advertisements?
questions.a: If you respect the royal figure, respect the product – its quality could not be questioned
questions.e: Maharaja Ranjit Singh appeared on a Manchester label.
